--- title: "What are Networks?" format: revealjs: scrollable: true theme: default css: ucla-theme.css width: 1280 height: 720 margin: 0.1 min-scale: 0.2 --- ## What is a network? - A set of entities - **Nodes**, **Vertices** - Joined via a set of relations - **Links**, **Ties**, **Edges** - In a **point and line plot**: - Entities are some shape (e.g., circles) - Relations are lines --- ## What is a network? - Don't confuse pictures of networks with the real thing! - In a **point and line plot**: - Entities are some shape (e.g., circles) - Relations are lines --- ## What is a network? - Lots of things in the world are networks ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## U.S. Airport Network ![](images/usairport.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"} --- ## GoT's Social Network ![](images/got.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"} --- ## The Brain's Neural Network ![](images/brain.jpg){fig-align="center" width="80%"} --- ## The Network of Psychological Symptoms ![](images/symptoms.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"} --- ## The Body's Organ Network ![](images/body.jpg){fig-align="center" width="80%"} --- ## Defining Social Networks - Networks are everywhere, but only a specific subset of them is actually a social network. - A network is **"social"** if it involves people (or groups) and their thoughts, interactions, and behaviors. - Even when we connect through technology (like texting or flying), it is the human interaction that makes it a social network. - In this class, we focus on the "purely social" elements: relationships, feelings, and how people exchange things. --- ## What is a social network? - Some networks are social networks - Schools, Workplaces, Instagram - Social networks link people via social relations --- ## What is a social network? - Some networks are both social and technological - Instagram, The WWW, Airports - Some networks are "purely" social - Schools, Workplaces In this quarter we will learn about **social network analysis (SNA)**. We will look mostly at "pure" social networks. --- ## The Roots of Social Network Analysis (SNA) - **Social Network Analysis (SNA)** is the main way we study these connections. - It grew primarily in the field of sociology, starting in the 1970s. - Today it is a team effort across different sciences, drawing on insights from multiple disciplines: - Sociology - Psychology - Anthropology - Communication --- ## What is a social network analysis? - SNA is an interdisciplinary field in social science in charge of studying social networks. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## The Big Picture: Network Science - SNA is just one branch of a much larger tree called **Network Science**. - Network Science studies all kinds of networks in the world. - This broader field includes experts from physics, computer science, biology, data science, and math. --- ## The Big Picture: Network Science ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## Summary - **Networks:** Systems of entities linked by relations - Different kinds: Social, biological, technological, etc. - **Social Networks:** Systems of interactive people (or groups of people) linked by social relations - **Network Science:** Interdisciplinary field in charge of studying all types of networks - Biology, mathematics, computer science, physics, etc. - **Social Network Analysis:** Interdisciplinary field in charge of studying social networks - Sociology, psychology, anthropology, communication --- ## The two faces of Social Network Analysis - SNA has two main faces; the first is **Network Theory**. - **Network Theory** explains how networks work and what they do to the people inside them. - It tries to answer big questions: Why do people connect? How do they behave? What are the consequences? - A great example is "social capital"—the idea that who you know brings you real-world benefits. --- ## The two faces of Social Network Analysis - The second side of SNA is **Network Measurement**. - This is where we use math and numbers to measure network properties. - Math helps us take "fuzzy" social concepts—like "popularity" or "social position"—and turn them into precise, measurable quantities. - These numbers allow us to predict why some people, companies, or countries succeed while others do not. --- ## The two faces of social network analysis ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: - **Theory:** General statements about how people behave in networks. - **Measurement:** Helps make natural language concepts more precise. --- ## Two mathematical representations of networks - Social Networks can be mathematically represented in two ways - We will learn how to go back and forth between the two: 1. A "Matrix" 2. A "Graph" --- ## Levels of Analysis in social networks ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: *We will be working through all these levels in the course! (But not in this order)* --- ## Zooming In: Micro Levels of Analysis - We can study networks by zooming in very closely. - **The Individual (Node) Level:** We examine a single person and their personal connections, collectively known as their **"ego network"**. - **Small Configurations (Dyad/Triad Level):** We look at relationships between two or three people. - At this level, we study things like how strong a tie is, or how small groups balance their friendships. --- ## Zooming Out: Macro Levels of Analysis - **Communities (Subgroups):** We look at larger clusters of people to see how close-knit they are. - **The Whole Network:** We look at the entire system to find large-scale trends, like whether the network is a "Small World". --- ## Three ways of talking about "social networks" - **Social network theory** is a branch of social science that uses natural language and intuition to describe real-world human interactions. - Its concepts can be vague. - **Graph theory** is a branch of pure mathematics that uses less ambiguous terms to define "analogues" of these fuzzy social network concepts. - **Matrix algebra** is a branch of applied mathematics that links graph theory concepts to allow for calculations and the development of metrics for social network ideas (like "centrality"). --- ## The "Three-Step Shuffle" - A major goal of learning SNA is mastering three different ways to view networks: 1. Seeing networks as real-world human interactions. 2. Seeing networks as mathematical graphs. 3. Seeing networks as quantitative data tables (matrices). - Transitioning smoothly between these three views is the key to understanding how networks work and change. --- ## The "Three-Step Shuffle" ![](images/three-step.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
